utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers. It's for you to make your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Just for the record, Stephen Sayers, presenting the opening statement for the accused Dario Kordic. I will be assisted today at points during this presentation by Mr. Naumovski and my colleague Mr. Browning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long do you anticipate being?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would suspect that this would go a substantial part of the day but not beyond, Mr. President. I will handle most of the presentation, but let me, if I may, just explain the division of the presentation. Mr. Naumovski will handle some of the political/historical background. Let me just say, Mr. President, that we do not propose to go back 500 years or even 50 years but, rather, two or three years before the 1990 elections. Mr. Naumovski will explain the political evolution of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the local evolution of that party in Busovaca and Mr. Kordic's role in it, and he will also cover political activities and Mr. Kordic's activities in Busovaca pre-referendum, that is, before February the 29th and March the 1st, 1992. Mr. Naumovski will also give a presentation of the evidence we expect to adduce regarding Mr. Kordic's personality, character, and background, and he will also cover events in the turbulent period in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, what concerns me is the way that you propose to deal with this. What, if my recollection is right, the Rule allows is a statement, and you propose to make four or so. Again, speaking from my experience, I've never come across a case conducted in this way, that a number of people make statements. Also, you haven't asked the leave of the Court to do it. I've discussed it with the Trial Chamber. We propose to allow, on this occasion, since you're prepared in this way to deal with it, but in future, if you want to make four speeches as opposed to one, then you must apply to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The reason we had done it this way was that we appreciate, obviously, a day of an opening statement is difficult to follow, and we had hoped to break it up to make it more interesting for the Trial Chamber, and we would cover different points. We're not going to duplicate the presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But let me just address one point, Your Honour. I want to say this at the outset: We have previously assured the Court that we are going to try to present the evidence on behalf of Mr. Kordic in the most expeditious way. There are a lot of witnesses on the witness list, and you have actually asked us to address the number of witnesses that we have listed. We've done a written submission on that. Let me say though, many, many of these witnesses are going to be very short on particular evidentiary issues. Let me also say, and I hope this does not revisit me in an unpleasant way in the future, but we fully intend to be finished with Mr. Kordic's evidence by the August recess or a month earlier if possible. If we can expedite the presentation of evidence, obviously subject to considerations of witness availability, which is the principle reason why our witness list is so long. We're not sure, and I'm sure the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution is aware of the difficulty of getting witnesses from Bosnia-Herzegovina, our first-choice witness may not always be available, so we may have to use one or maybe two witnesses to adduce evidence on that particular point. We do not anticipate that that's going to be a problem, but just to be careful, we have outlined for the Trial Chamber the entire universe of witnesses from whom we expect to adduce evidence. In so doing, we've actually made, I regret to say, quite a bit of work for ourselves, because we had to do prospective summaries of the evidence of all of these witnesses, and we decided to do it all at once so that the Trial Chamber has them all instead of into two stages, as we were permitted to do. But as I say, we will try to be through in four months at the outside, and we believe that we can be through in three months, provided we coordinate shortly with the Victims and Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- provided we can obtain access to transcripts from other cases in an expeditious way, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- that are produced in response to our request for subpoenas, and also, provided that we can acquire the affidavits that are anticipated by Rule 94 ter, a Rule with which we intend to comply to the letter, if at all possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, while you mention that, I think it's more important that you have the affidavits in some form and you apply the Rule to the absolute letter. I would regard it as a matter in which there should be some latitude because of the difficulties we've seen of obtaining them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. We have given thought to that, Mr. President, and as I say, we do not presently anticipate tremendous difficulties acquiring the written evidence. We appreciate the considerations of expediency and acceleration of these proceedings that that Rule provides, and we'll do our level best to try to present the affidavits in corroboration of live witness's testimony before the live witness testifies, to the maximum extent that we can. Let me just start, if I may, by revisiting one of the contentions made in the Prosecution's opening statement a year ago. A contention was made that the absence of documents -- that the absence of statements could be somehow construed as evidence of culpability in a case where the evidence, or much of it, goes both ways. Against that, let me just make a preliminary observation that few, if any, wars certainly in recent history, few, if any, wars such as the civil war that was fought in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, 1993, and the first part of 1994 have ever been fought in an atmosphere of such pervasive surveillance, evidence collection and spying. The press was present throughout this civil war, not just members of the international press from many countries but also the press from organs of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, press from the organs of the government of Herceg-Bosna. The military intelligence units of UNPROFOR, BritBat, DutchBat, the ECMM, Com Brit For, were all keeping their intelligence ears and eyes open. The military intelligence cells, as the Court knows, were making daily, weekly, and monthly intelligence reports of all significant developments and events in Bosnia-Herzegovina generally, and Central Bosnia generally, and in the municipalities at issue in this amended indictment specifically. These reports were updated and revised to reflect a cumulative understanding of events, at least from one perspective, a western perspective, in a situation where complex and confused political and military developments were occurring. The Court will recall the numerous intelligence-gathering resources deployed by the ABiH, and we expect to produce evidence relating to these. On a small scale, you have the intelligence resources in Stari Vitez. The witnesses who have already testified have established this; Mr. Rebihic, Mr. Kalco, on a small scale, as I say, keeping a very complicated, detailed diary of daily events not merely on a daily basis but sometimes on an hourly and even on a minute-by-minute basis. Videotapes were made, I must say, of all significant speeches and pronouncements specifically made by Mr. Kordic, and as the Court well knows, the videotape evidence, what he said or what he is, more accurately, said to have said is very much a significant issue in this case. But the evidence is that all comments made on television, all public pronouncements made by Mr. Kordic and by others, were recorded and the contemporaneous reports of these statements, these speeches, these public positions taken by political and military figures, were duly passed up the chain of command and submitted to the 3rd Corps headquarters in Zenica. You also have, as the Court recalls, the Agency for Investigation and Documentation, the State Commission on Gathering Facts on War Crimes, and the Court has seen evidence of some of the products of the investigations of these institutions. We expect to present some more. There was a war crimes indictment against Mr. Kordic and a number of other people, as the Court well knows, in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the end of 1993, and evidence collection, on a substantial level, was part of that indictment. I say that simply to make this point and the point that will be made by the Defence's evidence, that there was and could have been almost nothing that occurred of a public nature that escaped scrutiny or notice, that was not videotaped, recorded, reported upon and summarised. Yet, and I ask this rhetorically, where is the evidence of Mr. Kordic doing what would be necessary to make him guilty of war crimes? Are there any orders in evidence of Mr. Kordic to others to commit war crimes? No. Are there any orders that Mr. Kordic issued to military units after the organisation of the HVO had proceeded to the point of a hierarchical, recognisable chain of command? And we will present evidence as to when that occurred. And the answer to that question, I believe, also is "No." Is there evidence, written or otherwise, of Mr. Kordic actually giving orders to anyone? The evidence is that he did not. Similarly, the Court must ask itself, in a case of this nature, what is the evidence of Mr. Kordic uttering table-pounding speeches, giving speeches peppered with violent invective, advocating armed combat, armed conflict violence? We would submit to the Trial Chamber that actually when you take a look at the evidence, and we will produce more videotapes of what Mr. Kordic said, more articles of reporting upon what he said, there is none. You can see the videotapes for yourself, you can read the articles for yourself. The Court will recall that the best evidence of what he said is what he said, and it's not recollections of people given through oral testimony who have lived through a civil war, who have lost family members, and whose recollection is naturally filtered through a veil of embittered recollection. One good example is Witness AQ, a witness from Ahmici, and I'll discuss that and the evidence that we expect to introduce on that subject in just a few seconds. But the point is that the Defence of Mr. Kordic expects to show -- and the Prosecution has not shown to date -- that there were no contemporaneous speeches, no reports of speeches containing intemperate comments on his part. In fact, the reverse is true. The Court takes a look at the speeches. They usually incorporate political views on subjects of significance to the local community, to the regional community in the Lasva Valley, occasionally on developments of national significance, in his view, to his country, Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those views are usually expressed, and, in fact, we would think the evidence will show, always expressed in a calm, rational, and measured way. Let me just explain to the Trial Chamber the points upon which we intend to present no evidence. I'll spend a little time on that. And we are obliged, if I may say, to the Trial Chamber for issuing its April the 6th, 2000, decision on the accused's motions for judgements of acquittal. Paragraph 32 of the decision is at the heart -- what this case is really all about. The Trial Chamber observed there that the Prosecution relates to the participation of the accused in the highest levels of government and the Defence should prepare its case accordingly. And I wish to assure the Trial Chamber that we have taken that observation to heart, and we will try to do precisely that over the course of the next three months, I hope, four months if necessary. Before I outline what that evidence is, the Trial Chamber also ruled that, in particular, the Defence will not be expected to call evidence concerning municipalities about which no evidence has been given, and we propose to call no evidence on 20 of the 22 municipalities listed in footnote 18 on page 10 of the court's decision. Let me just point out that the allegation in this case is of a widespread, systematic campaign of persecution throughout the territory of the HZ HB, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; and the HR HB, Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and also in the municipality of Zenica. Accordingly, we do not propose to introduce any evidence relating to approximately 70 per cent of that territory because the Prosecution did not introduce any, and we, therefore, do not believe that it would be appropriate to do so, and it's not necessary to do so. There are two exceptions to that rule, and let me just explain what those are. The municipalities of Bugojno and the municipality of Kakanj. The reason is that there was actually persecution in these two very important, strategic municipalities or persecution in the sense of harassment and large-scale evictions of civilian populations following military activity, but the evictions were of Bosnian Croat citizens by Bosnian Muslim armed forces. Now, let me also say that we could call much other evidence in the same vein throughout the territory of the HZ HB, the HR HB, and the municipality of Zenica, but I suspect the Trial Chamber would not let us do that, and those two exceptions to our general rule should make the factual point very well. There are three other points upon which we may call no evidence. The first, the municipality of Kresevo. I can inform the Trial Chamber that presently, we intend to introduce no evidence relating to this municipality because no evidence from the Prosecution has been put forward that Mr. Kordic was ever seen in the municipality of Kresevo in 1993 or indeed that he could even get there, because it was cut off from Busovaca by the Muslim armed attack on Bosnian Croat positions launched in January 1993 and resulting in the seizure of a seven kilometre stretch of the main supply route from Kacuni to Bilalovac. There is only one witness who testified about Kresevo, Witness E, and he merely described Mr. Kordic as a political figure, having no particular influence or authority in that municipality, and so it's our present intent not to call any evidence about Kresevo. Second, Zepce. We intend to call no evidence about this municipality. The Court will recall this has been described by a witness, Colonel Stutt, in the Prosecution's case, as the territory of one of Mr. Kordic's political rivals, Ivo Lozancic. Mr. Kordic's political influence did not extend to Zepce. As we understand the Prosecution's evidence, no contention was made that it did, and no Prosecution witness testified to the contrary, only two such witnesses having testified, Witness F and Witness AH. Similarly, there is no evidence that Mr. Kordic was ever seen in Zepce in 1993 or indeed, as I have said with respect to Kresevo, that he could even get there as a result of the isolation of the Bosnian Croat enclaves following the series of almost uniformly successful ABiH offensives in 1993. The third item about which we intend to call no evidence is Kaonik prison. The Trial Chamber has had no first-hand evidence connecting Mr. Kordic in any way with this military detention facility. The only evidence that the Court has heard is rumour and hearsay, and very frankly, we don't intend to waste any time on the subject. With the Trial Chamber's permission, at this point I'll just hand the podium over to Mr. Naumovski, who will describe the historical background of the political party and the political context of Mr. Kordic's initial activities within the political party, the HDZ, BiH, and our evidence on his family, character, and background. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. In our presentation, as we conceived it, we considered it necessary to say a few words about the historical and political context within which the events that are the subject of that case came to pass. I am not going to be too long, but I believe some facts need to be pointed out. In order to explain what happened during the critical period of time, I believe we need to say briefly how did the former state of Yugoslavia function. As is common knowledge, the former Yugoslavia was made of six republics, socialist republics, and even if it was a federation, those republics were all closely connected through the central government and central authority in Belgrade. The constitution of 1974 enabled -- gave republics larger autonomy, but one should know that in all those six republics and throughout the former Yugoslavia, only one party, that is, the League of Communists, enjoyed all the power and held all the power in its hands. That is why the life of people, ethnic minorities, in those republics seemed smooth and normal on the surface. One could not observe any differences between individual ethnic groups in public, and so on and so forth. It is curious that of those six republics, as many as five of them, in its name, reflected the name of the majority people. Only Bosnia-Herzegovina's name did not reflect the ethnic composition. Why? Because that republic had three sovereign peoples who enjoyed equal rights, Muslims, Croats, and Serbs. So that was the only republic in the former Yugoslavia in which all three peoples were constituent peoples of that state in every possible respect. Needless to say, when I speak about this, for all of you who were educated in accordance with standard criteria find it difficult to understand what for all of us who lived in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, what did a multi-party system mean, what the emergence of a number parties meant for all of us there, and I believe it will be difficult for you to understand all that followed, all that happened after the first multi-party elections in Yugoslavia. The multi-party system was introduced in Yugoslavia, if I may say so, in 1989, and at that time, a whole range of political parties were formed which expounded political programmes and so and so forth, as is the case in all the other democratic states. But -- and this is important -- the emergence of a number of parties or, rather, the end of functioning of one party which held everything under its sway, differences between individual ethnic communities and, therefore, individual republics in the former Yugoslavia began to emerge. Over the past -- over the previous 45 years or so, all those differences had been minimised, had been suppressed, kept at bay, and these problems, especially surfaced in the republics where there were members of several ethnic communities present. That holds true especially of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Unfortunately, when the results of the first multi-party elections were published, some forces headed by the former JNA and Greater Serbian hegemonistic tendencies refused to accept the election results and the decisions of peoples in individual republics who wanted the relations in the future in Yugoslavia to be governed by some other criteria, that is, in a much more equitable manner than the multi-party elections. To simplify matters, the same thing that happened at the level of former federal state of Yugoslavia was also happening and was repeated also in the territory of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Save that, what began there subsequently lended to much more severe consequences. What I'm trying to say: Although under the constitution of 1974, in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were three sovereign peoples and all three of them were the constituent parties of the then Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the moment when the former Yugoslavia began to burst at its seams as a federal state. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, there also emerged almost insurmountable difficulties among those three peoples. From the point of view of defence, it is important to know that the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina were the smallest ethnic community, that is, only 17.4 per cent, according to the population census of 1991. Because of their number, they were -- they were very concerned about not losing their right to equality with the other two peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina, who were the majority peoples there, because if they lost that equality that they used to enjoy, in view of their size, they would have been placed in an inferior position. In the light of those circumstances, it is important to understand the activities of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Mr. Kordic as one of its members. So that is a period of time when a state ceases to function, that is, the former Yugoslavia is falling apart, and the new state, which should substitute the former state, has not yet come to be, has not yet emerged. So this is a period of a vacuum, legal, political, and every other sense, because the old state has gone, the new state has not been born yet, but life goes on and never stops. So one had to provide some kind of organised life under the circumstances that existed at the time. Why was -- what were other idiosyncrasies of the situation in Bosnia? Because the republics of Bosnia and Slovenia had proclaimed their independence after their respective referenda, and on the 8th of October, 1991, Croatia, the Republic of Croatia cut short, broke its constitutional legal ties to the former SFRY. At the same time, in the then Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, those three constituent peoples, that is, Croats, the Muslims, and Serbs, conducted numerous political negotiations equally with the republics which had left the former Yugoslavia and those who were still part of the rump Yugoslavia and amongst themselves, endeavouring to win the best possible political option for their own ethnic community, for their own people. For instance, the Croats in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, apart from talks and contacts with other peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina, also held political talks with the representatives of the Republic of Croatia. On the other hand, representatives of Muslims in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and here it is perhaps particularly important to mention talks conducted by Mohamed Filipovic, who both secretly negotiated with Radovan Karadzic and Slobodan Milosevic about the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina remaining part of the rump Yugoslavia, as the term was coined, and on the other hand, they also conducted talks with the Republics of Slovenia and Croatia about Bosnia and Herzegovina possibly creating a community with those two republics. Regrettably, as far as we know, it is Alija Izetbegovic, who rejected the possibility of Bosnia-Herzegovina forming a kind of alliance with the Republics of Slovenia and Croatia, evidently in the belief that the then Yugoslav People's Army would help and contribute to preserve Bosnia-Herzegovina, if I may put it that way. In that highly delicate situation, which is an exception to the rule in the political environment, one should view the activities of Mr. Dario Kordic, in the Croat Democratic Union in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a Croat from that area, together with other politicians in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he was simply looking, searching the option that would suit best the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were all possibilities on the table except one, and that was that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, after the Republic of Croatia left the former Yugoslavia, the Croats did not want to remain in the -- in what remained of the former Yugoslavia. Unfortunately, as I've said, some forces could not accept the -- could not come to terms with the results of elections in some of the republics, so that the JNA, of course, and the politics of -- the policies of Slobodan Milosevic, so that first the Republic of Slovenia was attacked and then the Republic of Croatia. And if the war in the Republic of Slovenia could be settled, been very short, did not inflict any particular casualties or destruction, the war in Croatia produced most disasters relative to the country disastrously, and there were very many casualties, including among the civilian population and citizens who, of their own will, undertook to defend their fatherland, building at the same time the Croatian army. Your Honours have already heard that among those people who had decided to -- who volunteered to defend their country, there are also very many people from Bosnia-Herzegovina, not only Croats but Muslims as well. Needless to say, in parallel with that war and, as an effect, the corollary of this war, numerous forces, troops, and armaments of the JNA pulled out of the Republic of Croatia into the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was quite obvious then, and quite clear also, that the JNA would not allow the whole population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, all the three sovereign and equal people, decide on their fate by themselves and how they would regulate their mutual relations in a future state as they would like to. And these misgivings came true because the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were led by the Serb Democratic Party openly said -- stated that they would not stay in an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, so those forces, through a military action or, rather, by force and in a highly undemocratic way, wanted to prevent the other two peoples from deciding on their own about their fate. At the height of fighting in the Republic of Croatia, as Your Honours know, a day after -- in spite of the fierce resistance, the town of Vukovar in the Republic of Croatia fell. On the 18th of November, 1991, the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina formed the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, and about a week before that, on the 12th of November, '91, the Croat Community -- Croat Posavina, which is the northern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was formed. Those two communities performed as political, cultural, and economic entities, and in this manner the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which at that time only on paper, simply publicly announced the idea of forming a community through which and into which the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina would preserve their ethnic identity and their interests, which at that time began to diverge. During the Prosecution's case, the Prosecutor pointed at the political activity of the Croat Democratic Union in Bosnia-Herzegovina and these subsequent organs of authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina and tried to present it as if they were acting under completely sterile positions, if I may put it that way. However, this has nothing to do with the real life, with what existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina in real life. Meanwhile, when the war broke out in the Republic of Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina was still a socialist republic with a government formed jointly by the three so-called national -- rather ethnic parties which had won elections held in November 1990. At first, they indeed worked in unison and that government functioned, and their cooperation did yield some fruit. But as the time went by, it became more and more evident that it was only a fictitious cooperation, and it stopped in October 1991 when the representatives or one of the three coalition partners or, rather, the representatives of the Serb Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina left the -- walked out of the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the debate about the referendum that was to take place about the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was as of that day that we could say legal authorities -- legal organs of power elected in the elections of 1990 ceased to exist. At the time when these Croat communities that I spoke about were formed, the Serbs in the Serb Democratic Party quit all the authorities, all the bodies of authority in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And from the point of view of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not only did the former state, the socialist Yugoslavia, cease to exist, but even that socialist Bosnia-Herzegovina was not in existence any longer because the election results of 1990 had been annulled by the decision and by date of illegal or unlawful moves of representatives of one people or, better said, the system within Bosnia-Herzegovina fell apart, disintegrated. This resulted in a political crisis, naturally, and among the smallest people, that is, the Croats, it added to their fears because they were quite aware of secret negotiations that the Muslims were conducting about remaining within the former Yugoslavia, that is, within the state which was made of Serbian Montenegro. The Prosecutor, during the presentation of their case, repeatedly went back to a meeting that took place in the office of the late president of Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, on the 17th of December of 1992. Mr. Kordic's Defence believes that the talks and political options on the table at that meeting were basically interpreted in a wrong way, were misinterpreted, and the talks held on that occasion we do not think can be related in any way whatsoever to what came to pass a year or two later. Another meeting, and it is very important from the point of view of our Defence, another meeting was held before the referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina decided on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Moreover, at that meeting there was only talk about possible political options if other peoples opted for something else. As I said, it was common knowledge that there were quite a number -- there was a whole gamut of options on the table, and that would be quite normal, and coming from the point of view of western democracies. But all these options, all these ideas that were also raised at that meeting, only a third of support was the basis for negotiations with the other two constituent peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and all those options, all those ideas, should have been translated into life only by political means and not by force or any other uncommon means, and that is very important to point out from the point of view of Mr. Kordic's Defence. Needless to say, as the case is conducted against Mr. Dario Kordic, and I speak here on his behalf now, we think that it is of utmost importance to analyse specifically the behaviour, the conduct of Mr. Dario Kordic, as an individual, and we believe that one needs to analyse only what he said and the ideas that he promoted. And what he did needs to be separated from the ideas, thoughts, and activities of some other people and, after all, from any other Croat politician who attended that meeting and were politically active in Bosnia-Herzegovina and even in the Lasva Valley, where Mr. Kordic was active. We deem it of consequence to completely, unambiguously and precisely determine what the political duties were and when did Mr. Dario Kordic discharge. In our view, this means that we are going to prove, and that is our duty, that Mr. Kordic held no military duties, nor did he discharge any administrative duties, rather duties such as members of the government of the HVO or some other bodies had. We therefore believe, and we shall be pointing out that during the presentation of our case, that at a point when a state is disappearing, that is, the former Yugoslavia, and a different state, a new state, has not yet emerged, then any political option which was promoted or, rather, considered by the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including Mr. Kordic, among other people, was quite legitimate and quite lawful, because each one of these options pursued only one thing, and that was to protect the interests of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina; not, however, at the expense of the other two peoples, but to find a modus operandi to coordinate its relations, to harmonise its relations with the other two peoples, yet not at the expense of the Croat people. When I said about certain misgivings, about certain fears that the Croats in Bosnia felt, I perhaps need to say that for the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the war and the state war began in September 1991, actually, when the JNA razed to the ground the Croat village of Ravno, which, however, they did not provoke any official reaction of the then authorities, as if it had never happened. Let me try to now sum up what I tried to say about the activities of Mr. Kordic. The Defence believes that the political activities of Mr. Kordic should be considered in two completely different political and temporal contexts. The first temporal context or, rather, the political framework or, rather, the first period of time is the period of time when it is said -- that is the period of time when the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina still existed formally and was still legally part of what remained of Yugoslavia, and when the negotiations involved -- when the negotiations addressed different options, different modalities of the relation of -- relations in a future state, which is quite a democratic manner of thought, because they pursued a political solution, a political solution to the regulation, to the organisation of the state in which all those three peoples would live. Naturally it is the right of every individual and every people, therefore, to try to advocate and win the best possible options for this, and this was the gist of the political election of Mr. Kordic. And the end of it came at the time of the referendum at which the Croats and Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina voted "yes" for an independent sovereign state. I believe Your Honours will remember that during the cross-examination of Witness O, we submitted an Exhibit 74/1 in which we showed that various Croats and Muslims in Busovaca and those involved in the political life in Busovaca, Dario Kordic, Husnija Neslanovic, Zoran Maric, Asim Sunulapasic, and a number of others, and that he also put his signature as a public manifestation of their wish to have Bosnia-Herzegovina proclaimed a sovereign state. As is known, the referendum took place on the 29th of February and the 1st of March, 1992, and at that referendum the Muslims and Croats invested a joint effort to ensure that Bosnia-Herzegovina becomes an independent state in a legal, lawful, and legitimate manner. And this is what entitles me to say, I believe, that it is quite wrong and unfounded to claim that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in fact, pursued the disintegration of Bosnia-Herzegovina so as to supposedly, allegedly, join the Republic of Croatia and so on and so forth, because had the Croats not taken part in the referendum, Bosnia-Herzegovina would not have become an independent state and, moreover, would have legally remained part of what remained of the former Yugoslavia or, rather, the rump Yugoslavia. So that could be called the first stage, the first temporal framework in which Mr. Kordic was politically active. The second period of time begins after the referendum. All of the efforts of Mr. Kordic and the Croat Democratic Union in Bosnia-Herzegovina, of which he was a member, were focusing on the regulation of relations amongst the peoples who lived within the territory -- in the territory of the newly-proclaimed Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and not outside the borders or beyond the borders of that republic. That this is so emerges clearly from the decision on the foundation of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, which says that it is founded within the state and legal borders of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and constitutes its integral part. So in our submission, it is very important to bear this in mind, that there were two periods of his activity, because in the presentation of the Prosecution case -- and obviously they had the right to present it in the way they wanted to -- this was completely omitted, and I think that it is very important to understand the conduct of Mr. Kordic in his political activity. However, there was an additional problem within Bosnia-Herzegovina which the Defence has to keep pointing out. Bosnia and Herzegovina declared its independence in early March 1992, but this declaration was exactly this, a pure declaration. Regardless of the fact that the United Nations, on the 22nd of May, 1992, recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina, unfortunately Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the time of its declaration as an independent state, did not have all the institutions that a modern state should have, if we look at the western standards. After a month of its declaration of independence, Bosnia and Herzegovina experienced an aggression of the JNA and the Bosnian Serbs led by the Serbian Democratic Party. So that at the very beginning of its existence which was to take hold, about 70 per cent of its territory was cut off from the central government in Sarajevo. That capital was besieged and cut off from the rest of the country so that Bosnia-Herzegovina, at the time when it was formally declared an independent state, did not exist in reality. There was no central government, there were no communication lines, and the legal institutions were unable to function properly. And this was due to the chaos which ensued after the certain territories were cut off. Certain communities tried to make political arrangements which were possible at the time, and the Trial Chamber, I think, has had ample opportunity to understand that. The political life continued in separate municipalities in the best way possible at the time. In my introductory remarks, I will only say -- I will make a couple of more points on Mr. Kordic as a person. Mr. Kordic was born on 14 December 1960, in a Catholic family in Sarajevo. Mr. Kordic's mother was a physician, and his father was a veterinarian. At first the family lived in Zepce, where the father worked as a veterinarian, and his mother worked as a general practitioner. Then she got a specialisation in Busovaca as a paediatrician, and that is when they moved there, and they continue to live there today. In addition to Mr. Kordic, Mr. Kordic's parents had four other children. Even though we consider it irrelevant for these proceedings, we felt compelled to present evidence that the Kordic family had never had any blood ties with Mr. Mate Boban, because a number of Prosecution witnesses testified to that. We will produce witnesses from both the Kordic and Boban families and will provide evidence that no blood ties exist between these two families. But let me just add a couple of other things in regard of Mr. Kordic. He went to the elementary school in Zepce, and after the family moved to Busovaca, he completed his primary schooling in Busovaca. In 1979, he graduated from the high school in Vitez, and the Trial Chamber had an opportunity to hear from one of his teachers there. He then went on to Sarajevo to study political science and graduated in Sarajevo with honours. He received a golden badge, which is one of the awards. Then he started the study of international affairs, which did he not complete, because he then took a job in company Vatrostalna. In 1986, he married Vernera Kordic, born Krilic, who worked as a psychologist and worked as a child psychologist in Kaonik and held that job throughout the war, commuting to Kaonik. Three children were produced in this marriage, the son in 1987, and the next child in 1992, and the youngest in 1995. Throughout Mr. Kordic's activity in Busovaca, the entire family continued to live in Busovaca, both his parents and other family. Since 1995, the Kordic family has lived in the city of Zagreb. As I pointed out, Mr. Kordic was born and raised in a Catholic family, and these were the principles that were observed, and this is how he was raised, and this is how he raised his own family. Because of his Catholic upbringing, Mr. Kordic never had any bad word about any other ethnic groups. I had an opportunity to talk to a number of people who were Mr. Kordic's neighbours, and I never met any person who would say anything contrary to the conclusions which I have reached on Mr. Kordic. Even the Muslim witnesses here not only spoke well of his neighbours but also who was prepared to assist people and help him anyway he could if they asked him. This same attitude governed Mr. Kordic's conduct in politics. He never used any pejorative or disrespectful words in regard of any other ethnic group. It is important to point out that he did not do that even at the time, during the period of ten months when Croats in the Lasva River valley were completely cut off from the rest of the world, and when, on a daily basis, they did not know what tomorrow would bring and whether they would survive to see the next day. Even during his time in Vatrostalna where he worked as a journalist, Mr. Kordic was politically active, and he continued to do so when, after about 45 years, the multi-party system was reintroduced in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Pero Kordic, Mr. Kordic's father, was one of the founders of the HDZ, and Dario Kordic followed in his father's footsteps. I think that I just need to point out a few highlights of his career. In September of 1991, in the conference in Busovaca, he was elected the head of the party. After the first multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Kordic became this head of the defence in the local government. This department had nothing to do with the military structure, and the military structure, at that time, in existence was still the JNA. In this post, Mr. Kordic opposed the efforts of the JNA to mobilise military recruits who were of Croatian and Muslim origins. This was a dangerous period, because the JNA had the presence in Busovaca until May of 1992. Mr. Kordic was elected president of the HDZ for Busovaca in 1991, and was in this duty until April 1992, when he was replaced by Florijan Glavocevic. In April 1992, in the second conference of HDZ, he was elected one of the five vice-presidents of HDZ, along with Mile Ekmescic, Pero Markovic, Jadranko Topic, and Ivo Zivkovic. Of course, the Trial Chamber had opportunities to learn that on 18 November 1991, when the Herceg-Bosna was established, he was elected one of the two vice-presidents. The president was Mate Boban, and the other vice-president was Bozo Rajic. I think that I will end here in order not to take any more time, and later on I will add a few more comments. Thank you very much for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, taking up directly from where Mr. Naumovski left off, I'd like to address what we intend to be or expect to be the evidence presented by Mr. Kordic relating to his participation in the highest levels of government, that is, in the HZ HB and the HR HB. I'll proceed then to discuss the persecution theory and the evidence that we expect to produce on that, and then I'll summarise the evidence that we expect to produce from our witnesses on the chain of command. And as I've previously informed the Trial Chamber, our first witness also address that, but they'll also address, inferentially, the other issues that I've just mentioned. Now, turning to the HZ HB, the Court well knows this was formed on the 18th of November, 1991. We have previously gone over, with the constitutional expert from the Prosecution, Dr. Ribicic, the significant developments in the HZ HB. As the Court knows, the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO, was formed on April the 8th, 1992. Now, the Court may wonder, what did the HZ HB do between the date of its foundation and the date of the establishment of the HVO? The evidence will show, I think, that it didn't do anything. It held two informal meetings of the HZ HB, but they were held simultaneously with party meetings of the HDZ, BiH, and no legislation was adopted, no organisational steps were taken. It existed really no more than as a paper entity until one of the watershed states that we've previously covered, which was July 3rd, 1992, where there was a meeting of the Presidency of the HZ HB and the first set of legislative measures were adopted. But with respect to the period November the 18th, 1991 to July 3, 1992, I think the Trial Chamber can well see, and the evidence will show, that this organisation, this entity, was no more than a loose association of approximately 30 municipalities. We've already identified those. They are mentioned in paragraph 5 of the amended indictment. The Court has already heard evidence, and we intend to present more, that the internal governance of this association was rudimentary in the extreme. The Court will have in mind the initial organisational document, Exhibit Z27.2. Three portions I would like to draw the court's attention to. First, Article 5. This community was organised to respect the democratically elected government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as long as it remains an independent state. And I emphasise this was before the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had come into existence, before the referendum had even been passed on that issue. The second Article, Article 6, was that the community was to respect all valid international regulations that constitute the basis of contemporary civilised relations in society, but more importantly, insofar as the highest levels of government are concerned, to the respect that that entity could have a government at that time, Article 7 stated that the supreme authority of the community would be reposed in a presidency. The post of president of the HZ HB did not exist initially, until July 3, 1993. Instead, there was a presidency. And the Presidency consisted, Your Honours, of the most senior representatives of the Croatian people in the various member municipalities or the presidents of the HDZ, BiH municipal boards. And Mr. Kordic was one of these representatives, one of 30 or so, 30 or more. As the Court knows, initially, Mate Boban was elected the president of the community, and he remained the president of the community until the foundation of the republic, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, on August 28, 1993. Indeed, even following the foundation of that republic, directly against the context of the Owen-Stoltenberg plan, Mr. Boban remained the president of the republic until he resigned at a meeting in Livno on the 8th of February, 1993 -- 1994, I'm sorry. We expect to have evidence from people who were at that meeting, who will explain the circumstances of his resignation, and we intend to produce members of the HZ HB and HR HB who will discuss the functions of the president at the time that he held the office, and also the functions, of course, of the members of the Presidency before July the 3rd of 1992 and thereafter. After the HVO was formed -- let me just say -- as I've said, the HVO was formed on April 8, 1992, following the vote that established the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And as the Court knows, the Croats did participate in this referendum, and that produced a 99.44 per cent vote of the people who actually voted. Now, it's material to note that the Bosnian Serb population, almost to a man and almost to a woman, abstained, boycotted this referendum. So 35 per cent of the entire population essentially refused to vote, and that was an extremely ominous augury of the future in the country in light of the events that Mr. Naumovski has just gone over. The Republic was formed on March 6, 1992. Ten days later, the evidence will show that the Bosnian Serb army attacked Mostar. Two or three weeks after that, the BSA attacked Sarajevo. Quite simply, the organs of central government of this brand new republic never had the opportunity to be established. They never really had the opportunity to get off the ground, and they never functioned. The Court might well ask itself of the plight in which the various municipalities of the entire country, not merely the HZ HB, found themselves, cut off from the central government and left to fend for themselves, and facing a determined, well-financed, very well-equipped adversary, which, I might add and must stress, had an extensive cadre of very well-trained officers, former JNA officers; a solid military organisation; and a solid background of logistics, supplies, and equipment, experience. This entity rapidly launched a series of successful offensives. These offensives produced extremely large waves of refugees and one statistic that is recited in a document that we will introduce into evidence, a United Nations Commission on Human Rights report, dated November the 17th, 1993, captures perhaps the magnitude of the humanitarian disaster that was wrought as a result of this incipient and ultimately full-blown civil war. Of a total population of 4.2 million Bosnian, Serbs and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, by the end of 1993, 2,1 million people had been displaced, 50 per cent of the population, and the evidence will show what kind of an impact that had upon the resources of the areas where these refugees had to flee, where they were compressed into approximately 30 per cent of the territorial area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This posed an enormous strain upon the fabric of society, and it quite simply broke down. There was competition for basic resources, housing, food, clothing, and we believe the evidence will show and the Trial Chamber will be convinced that the institutions of civilised society simply fractured under the enormous strains of these influxes of refugees, with the resulting outbreak of lawlessness, inability to control the rising tide of lawlessness, and indeed the Court will hear evidence from police chiefs that we intend to call from various municipalities to explain precisely that. They will explain that their forces, the police forces, were actually depleted as a result of having to send people to fight on the front lines with the Bosnian Serb army. And these weren't simply military police. These were representatives of the civilian police. On April the 8th of 1992, the Presidency of this fledgling republic issued a proclamation of an imminent threat of war, and it was on that same day that the HVO was formed. This decree was signed by Mr. Boban not at a meeting, I might stress and the evidence will show, not at a meeting of the HZ HB Presidency, but he just signed it himself in Mostar on April the 8th of 1992. Mr. Kordic was not present at that time. But two points are material with respect to the HVO, Mr. President. The first is that the HVO would be the supreme defence body of the Croatian people and the HZ HB, and this is already in evidence at Exhibit 182/1, tab 1, a very short document. But the second paragraph of this founding document I think is significant and merits the Trial Chamber's careful consideration. The objective of this organisation was to take care of the sovereign space of the HZ HB and to protect the Croatian people as well as other peoples in the community that are attacked by an aggressor. It was a defensive organisation established to protect everyone. Now, the HVO, once again, was a very fledgling organisation in April, May, June and July. There was no military organisation. It had no rank structure. It had no general staff. It had no internal brigade structure. It was just an agglomeration of people with heterogeneous backgrounds, and one of them included -- or one of the people that was involved in the initial events was Mr. Kordic, but he was not a member of the HVO government at any time. He did not participate in the highest levels of the HVO government, especially after that government had been established in July of 1993. As to Mr. Kordic's political influence at this time, we expect the evidence to confirm the story that has already been established during the Prosecution's case. Consider Vitez, for example. Mr. Kordic had virtually no significant political influence in Vitez. In fact, most of the SDA political leaders on the civilian side had never even spoken to him, and that's established from the Prosecution case itself. But he did have influence in Busovaca, and Mr. Naumovski will address that at the appropriate time. But there's no question, Your Honours, that Mr. Kordic did, in April, May, June and July, take an active and vocal role to make sure that the Croat population did obtain their fair share of weapons stored in former JNA barracks as the JNA was withdrawing from the territory of Central Bosnia, and he was largely successful in this regard. And the Court will recall exactly how that occurred. We intend to produce evidence from people who were at these negotiations, and I stress "negotiations". There were negotiations that occurred between all of the parties, for example, in Novi Travnik in April of 1992 and, further, in Busovaca in May of 1992. And we expect also to produce evidence from the HVO military figures in these very early days, perhaps most notably Major-General Filipovic, to explain the context within which these discussions were occurring between the peoples who were attempting to obtain arms to defend themselves from what looked like an imminent assault. Some weeks ago, I reminded the Trial Chamber that a question was asked during the cross-examination of one of the Prosecution's witnesses regarding intertwining of civilian and political functions, and there was intertwining, as I informed the Presiding Judge, in the early months, once again, April, May, June, July of 1992, and there could hardly fail to be, because there was no separate civilian and military organisation. Everything was compressed together in a confused jumble in a time of military emergency and, I might add, looming humanitarian emergency. But our evidence will clarify for the Court, I trust, and early on in our case, in fact with the first few witnesses, I hope, what was established during Dr. Ribicic's testimony, and that is that the HVO slowly established itself into both a civilian structure and a military structure and the two were separate, and it's an unfortunate happenstance of terminology that the civilian government was called the HVO and that the military was called the HVO too. But the Court will recall that the civilian HVO ceased to exist following the foundation of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna when all the departments and governmental institutions that had been established over the preceding year were merged into the HR HB according to Article 46 of the basic decision. As of that time, September the 30th, 1993, the civilian HVO ceased to exist, but the military HVO continued on in existence. We urge the Court to consider the testimony of one of our first witnesses, Major-General Filip Filipovic, carefully. He will very graphically describe the turbulent beginning of the HVO, and also that turbulent beginning we expect to be confirmed by other high-ranking officers of the HVO general staff, whom we hope to be able to call during the course of this case, and also by high-ranking political figures who actually did participate in the government of the HVO, the HZ HB, and the HR HB. In fact, we intend to produce evidence from the individual that drafted most of the legislation that was adopted by the HZ HB. We hope to be able to introduce evidence from the people who participated at the highest levels of the Ministry of Justice or the Department of Justice, and they will explain also that within the HZ HB and within the HR HB, there weren't simply exclusively Croat people, people of Croat ethnicity, but people of Muslim ethnicity as well and some people of Serb ethnicity as well. Let me just turn to, if I may just before the break, the evidence that we expect to adduce through Major-General Filipovic. He's a retired major-general, having obtained that rank in the current Federation army. He served as Colonel Blaskic's second in command after June of 1992. He eventually replaced Colonel -- then General Blaskic as the Central Bosnia Operative Zone commander in April of 1994. He's a professional soldier. He was initially appointed, Your Honours, as the commander of the HVO armed forces in early April of 1992, one of the first commanders of the HVO armed forces. He will establish that when the civil war broke out, the Bosnian Croats had a grand total of about 10 professionally-trained military officers of Croat ethnicity available to them. He replaced Pasko Ljubicic, who himself had been a lieutenant in the JNA. He will also explain that because of his 20 years of military service with the JNA, having risen to the rank of colonel in that institution, he was viewed with some suspicion by his fellow Croats, he was not entirely trusted initially, and that he was replaced on May the 20th, 1992, by a gentleman named Zarko Tole. Mr. Tole unfortunately was captured during fighting with the Bosnian Serbs about ten days after his appointment. His replacement was another extremely short-lived individual by the name of Ivan Zorica, nicknamed Zulu, a man of no military experience, no strategic foresight, and he lasted 20 days in the position. This takes us to late May, June. It was Colonel Filipovic who recommended Colonel Blaskic to be the commander of the Operative Zone. Colonel Blaskic was a young officer, not immutably stained with JNA or former JNA ties. He had been trained in the JNA, but he was not so closely associated with the JNA as was Colonel Filipovic at that time. He was appointed commander of the Operative Zone in June of 1992. So as the Court can see from that brief recitation and, I think, the Court will accept as a fact that from April to June of 1992, the HVO found itself in a very chaotic organisational situation. But after this, an organisational framework began to be imposed in the armed forces of the HVO. Things began to settle down. Military men were inducted into the hierarchy and set up a chain of command. And one of them is the second witness we intend to call, a retired brigadier from the Federation army, Franjo Nakic, who was the third in command in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone and the chief of staff of the headquarters run by Colonel Blaskic. He had good organisational skills. He was a former major in the JNA reserve. He was brought in at the end of 1992, November 1992, to form the headquarter staff of the headquarters of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone at the Hotel Vitez, and he did so. These military men will provide evidence of how this military organisation was established, how it developed in a concrete way, how it adopted and enforced a code of military discipline, that this code worked. They will explain the staff organisation within the headquarters and within the armed forces generally and its command structure. They will explain how the brigades were formed on a municipality-based basis, reported up the chain of command to the headquarters in the Hotel Vitez. Each of the brigades were, in turn, organised into companies. We will also explain the formation of the so-called PPNs or special purpose units, and both of the soldiers will explain the command structure of those PPNs and also of the military police. And I might add that we intend to call two military police chiefs to eliminate any doubt that might be lingering, although I don't think any should be after the testimony of Witness AS, about the chain of command within the military police. One thing I want to say just before I leave this is that Mr. Kordic was nowhere in that chain of command after July the 3rd of 1992, [Realtime transcript read in error "November"] and it was on that date that the HZ HB came of age. If this is a convenient time to pause, I'll take that up after the break, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now. Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I may, two minor corrections for the record. I believe in Mr. Naumovski's recitation of the political issues connected with Mr. Kordic, he said that Mr. Kordic was elected vice-president of the HDZ, BiH in April of 1992. It should actually be November the 14th, 1992. And just in my concluding comments before the break, I said that Mr. Kordic was nowhere in the chain of command after July of 1992, and the transcript, page 47, line 24, reads November. It's with July that I'd like to address what we expect to show in our evidence. The Court knows that at a meeting held in Mostar on July 3, 1992, a new decision fundamentally pre-structuring the HZ HB was adopted. Mr. Kordic was at this meeting, and he was one of a hundred politicians, or a hundred or so politicians that attended. The Court will recall that this meeting occurred shortly after the declaration of a state of war in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the Presidency, that being June the 20th, just two weeks before. Once again, Article 5 of the decision that was amended repeated its respect for the democratically elected bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this time the newly established Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But the Article that deserves close attention from the Trial Chamber is Article 7, which wrought fundamental changes in the governance of this body. Supreme authority was now vested in the president of the HZ HB. This was a new office. The Presidency continued but its functions changed. Once again, the Presidency consisted of representatives of the Croatian people in the municipal bodies of authority or the senior officials thereof and also the presidents of the municipal HVOs. Once again, approximately 30-plus people in the Presidency. The Presidency was expressly to be a legislative body, Your Honours, a legislative body of the HZ HB, in turn to have a president, but this being a president of the Presidency as opposed to the president of the entity, although as a practical matter, the Defence would have to concede that these two offices, though conceptually distinct, were actually held by Mate Boban throughout. The Presidency was to have two vice-presidents, Mr. Kordic was one of them, Mr. Rajic was the other. It was also to have a secretary, that being, at all material times, Mr. Ignjac Kostroman. Article 8 of this new decision stated that the Presidency would appoint the executive and the administrative bodies of authority in the HZ HB; therefore, the legislature would appoint the government. And just several points that I would like to draw to the Trial Chamber's attention which we expect the evidence to establish and actually without controversion. First, obviously Mr. Kordic was not the president of the HZ HB and of course, never the president of the HR HB. He was only a vice-president of the Presidency. The Presidency was effectively a legislature, and the Presidency appointed the government. Now, we expect the Defence witnesses who participated in the highest levels of government to testify that Mr. Kordic played almost no role in that regard, Your Honours. He was never in the government of the HZ HB other than being a vice-president of the legislature and a legislator in his own right. The Trial Chamber will recall the emphasis placed in various papers submitted by the Prosecution and in argument upon the significance of the Presidency of the HZ HB. This entity met twice in the coming months, once on August 14, 1993, and Mr. Kordic attended that meeting. That meeting resulted in the appointment of the president of the civil HVO, Dr. Jadranko Prlic. The second time that the Presidency met was on October the 17th, 1993 [sic], which is the second watershed date of the HZ HB. The evidence is going to show, Your Honours, that thereafter, after October the 17th of 1992, not 1993, the Presidency of the HZ HB never held a session that Mr. Kordic attended until the foundation of the HR HB, nearly a year later. Now, as to the powers of Mr. Kordic, his political powers as a vice-president of the Presidency, there is not any doubt as to what those powers were. You've heard evidence from Dr. Ribicic, and you've actually considered -- you've seen the Code of Practice of the Presidency that was adopted on July the 3rd of 1992. The powers of vice-president of the Presidency were parliamentary. For example, in Articles 15 and 20 of that code, the vice-president could, in the absence of the president, call a session of the Presidency, but the evidence will show that Mr. Kordic never did so. Similarly, under Article 20, the vice-president, theoretically, could preside over a session of the Presidency in the absence of the president and exercise parliamentary power such as limiting addresses or holding addresses to a particular time limit, but the evidence will show that he never did that either. He never exercised these parliamentary powers. As I've said, he never attended any meetings of the Presidency after October the 17th of 1992, and there isn't going to be any doubt about that in the evidence. So that is the role that he played in the highest levels of government, if I may say so. We expect it to show it to be a zero role, actually. Now, a series of important organisational decrees were adopted on July the 3rd, and we've introduced some evidence of that in cross-examination and there will be no evidence relating to these decrees, and I'm not going to consume time by going over all of them, but I would like to emphasise just a few because these related basically to the HVO. The first decision was a statutory decision on the temporary organisation of executive authority and administration in the territory of the HZ HB. In other words, this decree set up the government and described what it would do, what its function was. First, under Article 2, the HVO was expressly defined as being a temporary body that existed in a time of war or an imminent threat of war and would cease to exist once the formal organs of civilian and executive and administrative power had been permanently established. Article 7 described how the HVO government was to be organised. At its head would be a president. There would be vice-presidents. There would then be department heads and other members. The organs of government at the highest levels were organised into six separate departments under Article 20. The Department of Defence, Interior, Economic Affairs, Finance, Social Affairs, and last, Justice and Administration. We expect to produce to the Court Ministers from these departments who will testify what they did, who directed their affairs, with whom they communicated, and most importantly, from the perspective of Mr. Kordic, his relative lack of prominence, in fact, complete lack of prominence the ordinary administration of the governmental affairs of the HZ HB, the operations of the president of the HVO, and of the departments. The second decision I would like to commend to the Court's attention was a decision that articulated the principle of transparency and a commitment that things would be done in public. All of the official acts of the organisation, decrees adopted by the HVO or HZ HB would be published publicly in a document called the Nadrodni List, and that's already been introduced into evidence. The Court will note, naturally, that it's a fairly significant document, containing many separate decrees, but for purposes of this case, only a few are significant. The first of those is a decree on the armed forces that was passed on July the 3rd, 1992. This was the first organisational effort undertaken by the government to regulate the affairs of the HVO armed forces. It defined the competencies of the HVO in Article 9. Competencies were to plan the defence of the HZ HB, to fund the defence of the HZ HB and provide mechanisms for that, to pass regulations relating to mobilisation of men of military age into the armed forces. Article 10 defined the competencies of the Defence Department, which was largely, in July anyway, to prescribe the structures of command and control of the armed forces. Significantly, Article 29 of this decree defined the competencies of the president of the HZ HB; not the Presidency but the president, the new office created on that date. It was the president who was the Supreme Commander of the armed forces. He had no ability to delegate his command function. It was the president who would draft regulations on military discipline, and, significantly, who would appoint and dismiss military commanders from duty. Article 31, of course, provided that command and control in the armed forces shall be implemented by the commanders of the armed forces in accordance with the powers given. The second significant decree, which I will merely mention and not examine in any detail because it's before the Court and its provisions say what they say, were the adoption of a decree relating to the rules on military discipline, very extensive in number and in scope. Some appointments were made to the government, Your Honours, on July the 3rd. Specifically, the Department of Defence was headed by Bruno Stojic, appointed on that date. As I have mentioned, the next meeting of the Presidency occurred just over a month later, August the 14th, 1992, and it was at that meeting that Dr. Prlic was appointed the president of the HVO, a position, I might add, that he retained until the foundation of the HR HB, until the Ministries of the HZ HB were folded into the Ministries or the departments of the HZ HB were folded into the Ministries of the HR HB. And Dr. Prlic was appointed the Prime Minister of the HR HB and, I believe, held that position from the 30th of September of 1993 until the end of the war and beyond. Of the people appointed to positions of authority within the HVO, the Court will no doubt recall that Mr. Kordic was not one of them. At no point was Mr. Kordic appointed to the position of president. He never held the position of vice-president of the HVO, any of the three. He never held the position of any department head within the HVO, at no time. The next watershed date in the evolution of this organisation was October the 17th, 1992, at a meeting of the Presidency of the HZ HB. Two vice-presidents of the HVO were appointed at that time, Mr. Valenta and Mr. Zubak. The Court will hear evidence relating to extensive revisions made to a new and sophisticated decree on the armed forces, delineating in far more detail the competencies of the Department of Defence and of the president. When I address the chain of command issues, the Court will recall that there has been some suggestion that the position of political commissar or zampolit of the type of political officer in the former armed forces of the Soviet Union was the model in the HVO. It was not. In fact, if you take a look at the decree on the armed forces, Article 25, political activity was expressly prohibited. Now, the Prosecution, as I said, has taken the position in this case that the Presidency of the HZ HB was omnipotent, omnipresent, and it must take that position in order to magnify and exaggerate Mr. Kordic's alleged political powers. We understand that. Must take that position because he was not involved in the military chain of command, as the evidence will establish. Must take that position because he was not in the government, the organs of civil government, let alone at the highest levels. But it should not escape the Trial Chamber's attention, and the evidence will establish this beyond doubt, that Mr. Kordic never actually attended a meeting of the Presidency after October the 17th, 1992, until the foundation of the HR HB. So the Court should ask itself: What did Mr. Kordic do as the vice-president of the Presidency after October the 17th, 1992? And our evidence will address that question and, I hope, answer it. He did play a prominent part in the establishment of the HVO government in Busovaca -- there is no question about that -- in May, June, July of 1992. But it will not escape the Trial Chamber's attention, I trust -- and Mr. Naumovski touched upon this lightly -- that he was not even the president of the HVO government in Busovaca at any time. That position was held initially by Mr. Glavocevic, and he was replaced, I believe in August of 1992, by Zoran Maric, who is currently a fairly prominent politician in Central Bosnia, in the Federation. It's our present intent, if we can, to call both of these politicians to explain to the Court precisely what the political evolution of the HVO was in Busovaca, who held power, and what they did. We expect that early on in the Defence case, the Court will be convinced by the evidence we expect to produce that the military and civilian functions of the HVO government, the HVO civil, the HVO military had largely and visibly diverged by October the 17th of 1992. The organs of civilian government had largely been created by that date, Mr. Kordic not being in them except as a member of the legislature and a vice-president of the Presidency. The organisation of the military was well along, and we expect to prove that in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Mr. Kordic was outside the chain of command, any chain of command, direct, indirect, and that will be confirmed by the military and civilian witnesses that we expect to call. Now, Mr. Kordic did participate in one committee of the HVO, and the Court will no doubt recall that evidence. It was a committee on personnel, he being one of five people on it, not the president of it. We do not believe that committee ever met, but the president of it is a man that we hope to be able to call in our evidence, and the Court will hear from him directly what that committee did and what role, if any, Mr. Kordic played in its operations. Suffice it to say, in the scheme of the HVO civil government, it was insignificant. It was not a department. It was simply a legislative committee, and you will hear the role that Mr. Kordic played on it, if any. As I transition from the HZ HB, Your Honours, into the HR HB, let me just focus on the Vance-Owen Plan about which you've heard evidence. This, of course, was one of a number of plans sponsored, considered, and approved by the International Community to try to bring an end to the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina generally, and that, of course, included Central Bosnia. Mr. Kordic, at no time, took any part in the negotiations that led to the Vance-Owen Plan. Mr. Boban, at all times, led those negotiations, but other people did participate, other prominent politicians of the Bosnian Croats, and we expect to call some of them, and you can hear from them directly what they did in connection with those negotiations and what was discussed and who was thought important to be present at these negotiations, and equally important, who was not. That's a general theme, I think, that has been fairly well established in the cross-examination case. Consider, for example, any of the conflicts that occurred in January or April of 1993. Was Mr. Kordic invited to any of the ceasefire negotiations by anybody? The Court might well ask itself: Was his name even mentioned in connection with these negotiations as someone who would be vital or even helpful? The answer to that is no. He did not attend any of these negotiations. He was not invited. He was not thought critical, important, necessary, or even helpful. He simply took no part in them. Now, the Vance-Owen Plan is noteworthy in several respects. As I've said, it was developed and ratified by the International Community. It envisaged the division of the country into ten provinces, but I confess I do not understand the argument made by the Prosecution that somehow these provinces were intended to be ethnically homogenous in some fashion, because the court can review for itself. In some ways it's a model of clarity. The government of the provinces, each one of them, including the ones at issue in this case, 3, 8, and most especially 10, were expressly and designedly multi-ethnic, not monoethnic. And it bears stress that the Croat contingent specifically and enthusiastically agreed to these proposals that had been developed by the International Community. Let me just review, for example, provinces 3, 8, and 10, the anticipated governments in each of these. Of course, they were to have Croat governors, but in province 3, the Bosanski Brod province, there was to be a Serb vice-governor and, I might add, an interim Provincial Government consisting of representatives of all three peoples, Serb, Muslim, and Croat. The same model applies to province 8, the Mostar province, which was to have a Croat governor, admittedly, but a Muslim vice-governor and a multi-ethnic interim Provincial Government. Now, with respect to province 10, the governor was to be a Croat, the vice-governor was to be a Muslim, and initially, there would be five Muslims who sat on the interim Provincial Government, four Croats, and one Serb. That was the model of the plan initially approved by the Croats, of course, that was in force until May of 1993, when the constitution of that interim Provincial Government was modified, there now being five Croats in the interim Provincial Government, four Muslims, and one Serb. The Court might ask itself: If Mr. Kordic was such a significant figure, participating at the highest levels of government, it follows, of course, that he would be recommended as the governor of this province, but you know that he was not. Vladimir Soljic from Bugojno was selected as being the governor designate, if you like, of province 10, and the members of the interim Provincial Government were listed on a document that we would like to draw to the Court's attention, Exhibit Z972, and there were five members, Mr. Valenta, Mr. Skopljak, Mr. Kordic, Mr. Ivan Sarac, and Mr. Zoran Perkovic. Accordingly, Mr. Kordic, as the Court can see, was anticipated to be one member of the five-member interim provincial government and not the governor. So even at the provincial or cantonal level, the role envisaged for Mr. Kordic was not that of a leader of the government but as one of the members of the government, if that model were ever to exist. And we know that it didn't. Unfortunately, the Vance-Owen Plan fell into disrepair after it had been rejected by the Bosnian Serbs at a parliamentary session held in the Republika Srpska on the 6th of May, 1993. I'd like to turn now to the HR HB, because that's the next logical progression. Following the Vance-Owen Plan's disintegration, if that's not too strong a term, the international negotiations, as the Court knows, continued. The International Community continued with its efforts to try to come up with some constitutional organisation, some governmental framework that would accommodate the interests of the three constituent peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you will hear from people who participated in those continued negotiations. Just as with the Vance-Owen Plan, Mr. Kordic was not one of them. He never was invited to participate in those negotiations and, in fact, did not. The Court knows the history of the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. I believe the latest report to the Security Council by the Secretary-General has already been introduced into evidence, dated August the 6th, Exhibit D141/1. That's a document that deserves some careful scrutiny.
