None mentioned Mr. Kordic's name as having anything to do with the events in Ahmici, and Mr. Kordic's name is, as to be expected, not mentioned in the report. Now, the HVO investigation was called for by Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart in a letter that he wrote to Colonel Blaskic on April the 22nd. Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart and Brigadier Duncan, the two soldiers who had primary military responsibility for BritBat and UNPROFOR in the Vitez area, never once spoke to Mr. Kordic about Ahmici, as was to be expected. But they did engage in extensive discourse with Colonel Blaskic on that subject. Colonel Stewart requested an investigation and testified that in order to have credibility, the investigating commission would have to have ABiH representatives on it. It should be, in other words, a joint commission. And one day later, Colonel Blaskic wrote back to him, saying, "We're ready to mount this joint commission." No steps were ever taken to constitute a joint investigative commission after that. The subject unfortunately never arose, and the reasons for that are, confessedly, unclear, and I'm obliged to say that I do not have -- I'm not in a position to say that we're able to offer a lot of evidence on why the joint commission idea just fell into desuetude, so to speak. I'm confused about it, because on April the 25th Mate Boban and President Izetbegovic signed a joint agreement where they both agreed to send a joint commission to investigate crimes or incidents that had occurred in the area of the Lasva Valley, and this was followed by a May the 1st, 1993, public announcement from the HVO public relations department in Mostar that an investigation was going to be done. One document has just recently surfaced from the United Nations Centre for Human Rights, written by the witness Mr. Akhavan actually before he visited Central Bosnia, and it establishes that the members of the ABiH were reluctant to participate on a joint commission because they saw this as perhaps resulting in a delay in what should be a prompt investigation. But the point is that apparently the ABiH was reluctant to and ultimately refused to participate in a joint commission, and that appears to be the case. It was confirmed by Lieutenant-Colonel Watters during his testimony at page 5867. There's no point, he said, in their view, of having participation in this commission because the crimes, presumably, were so clear. Well, the next thing that occurred is that Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart confronted Colonel Blaskic at his headquarters on May 9th, the Court will recall, May the 9th, 1993, in the company of Lieutenant-Colonel Duncan, challenged Colonel Blaskic, told him that he would appear in court one day, made a notation in his diary. Following this confrontation, Mr. Kordic arrived, but no mention was ever made of Ahmici after Mr. Kordic's arrival. Now, one day later on May the 10th, 1993, Colonel Blaskic did order the HVO Security and Information Service to conduct an inquiry. He instructed the SIS to gather information and to report back by May the 25th, 1993. I'm not going to spend any more time on this. Our arguments are contained in Confidential Annex 2. Much of this material was made the subject of closed-session testimony. I won't repeat it here. Our previous papers articulate the Defence position on that, and that remains our position. But the point is that the HVO was not able to interview eyewitnesses, it was not able to identify, with any degree of specificity, the precise perpetrators of the civilian killings and murders in Ahmici and, therefore, was not able to gain evidence beyond a reasonable doubt sufficient to punish the perpetrators. Since this was a military matter, as might be expected Colonel Blaskic followed up, issued another order on August the 17th, 1993, to the SIS, saying, "Follow up on this investigation, please." There is no evidence, I believe, that the SIS ever did so, or if they did, the results of that investigation are not available to us. We've not been able to uncover them. But there is no question that an investigation was done, as requested, and we believe that the testimony from, amongst others, Colonel-General Petkovic will confirm that. One point I would like to make is that Mr. Kordic was not involved at any stage in that investigation really. He had no legal responsibility or other responsibility to ensure that the military investigative machinery operated efficiently and continued to operate. Now, if I may, just in the interests of winding up, I'll turn to the evidence concerning the particular municipalities and the particular issues which we expect to adduce evidence on, just so the Court has an idea of where we're going.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: For that submission, I would like Mr. Browning to handle in a very expeditious way, 15 minutes or so, the evidence relating to the international armed conflict, the municipalities of Vitez and Kiseljak. Mr. Naumovski will then expeditiously handle Busovaca, and I'll handle the rest. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Let me, first of all, say that among the Kordic Defence team, that I will be the one person that will be responsible for making sure that our witnesses run smoothly and our case runs like clockwork, and I will do everything humanly possible to make sure we conclude our case by August, if not before. I say that because at the outset of Mr. Sayers' remarks, he pointed out that the division for the opening statement would be to make it interesting. What Mr. Sayers I'm sure has also got going through his mind, that my remarks, like finishing our case on time, that I will gladly abbreviate my remarks on the different municipalities and move as quickly as possible so we can finish the opening statement today and as expeditiously as possible. Let me, first of all, address the issue of the international armed conflict. As the Trial Chamber is well aware, the portions of the indictment that are based on Article 2, in order to establish a necessary prerequisite for that element of the indictment, the Prosecution must show the existence of an international armed conflict. We have previously filed a response to the Prosecution statement. That was filed this Friday. I think our remarks are succinctly set out, and I will be very brief. Let me just say this: that under the Tadic Appeals Chamber decision as well as a more recent Aleksovski opinion of the Appeals Chamber, it is the position of those two Appellate Chambers that for international armed conflict to exist, there must be a showing of an overall control of the HVO by the Republic of Croatia. We believe that the Prosecution has not made such a showing in this case. More importantly, as Mr. Sayers previously indicated, we will be calling a number of military witnesses in the Defence case, in our case, in chief, and we believe that when those military witnesses take the stand, whether it be General Petkovic, General Praljak, General Roso, when the Court has the opportunity to see those individuals testify, to hear their demeanour, they will realise -- you will realise that these individuals were not puppets of the Republic of Croatia. They were men of integrity. As well, this week the Court will hear the deputy commander under Colonel Blaskic. I think when you have an opportunity to look these military witnesses in the eye, you will see that these individuals were simply not puppets or marionettes of the Republic of Croatia. More importantly, when you have a chance to hear the testimony of these witnesses, it will be made clear that there were not HV troops in Central Bosnia. As Major-General Filipovic will testify this week, he wished there had been HV soldiers in Central Bosnia, because he could have used the help. They were getting the bejeezus beat out them in mid-1993 and could have used any assistance whatsoever, whether it be HV troops or not, and that simply was not the case. The troops were available from the Republic of Croatia in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Browning, can you confine your remarks to those of a forensic sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Judge May, Your Honour, Mr. President, I apologise that I tend to speak with a southern dialect from time to time, and I will try to tailor my southern expressions. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Or moderate your language.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Let me turn briefly from international armed conflict to the municipalities that I will cover. First of all, with respect to the municipality of Vitez, the Kordic Defence intends to put on minimal evidence with respect to the municipality of Vitez. We believe that counsel for Mr. Cerkez will cover this issue during their presentation. But we would emphasise to the Court that in our mind there has been a complete absence of proof with respect to Mr. Kordic's involvement and events in Vitez. Turning first to the incident concerning the municipal building and police station and its takeover June 19th, 1992, the testimony is clear that Mr. Kordic was not present during that event, and there's a complete lack of evidence as to his involvement in those incidents in June of 1992. Moreover, throughout the Prosecution case, as witness after witness has been presented concerning Vitez, it's clear that Mr. Kordic had no influence in that particular municipality, whether it be the testimony of Muhamed Mujezinovic, who has testified in virtually all of the Lasva Valley cases. He was a politician in the Vitez area and made it clear that Mr. Kordic had no influence in the Vitez area. The same is true of Munib Kajmovic. The same is true of Witness G, who described Mr. Kordic as simply a top person in the Busovaca HDZ. It's clear, when you go through witness after witness, that the Prosecution had testify concerning Vitez, Witness L, Witness N, Sulejman Kalco, Fuad Zeco, it is clear that Mr. Kordic had no influence in the Vitez municipality. Let me turn briefly to -- specifically to Ahmici. As Mr. Sayers has previously pointed out, in October 1992, we will present evidence that shows that there was heavy fighting in Jajce, that the ABiH intentionally ordered a blockade in Ahmici in order to prevent the movement of HVO troops, and that emphasises that there was a strategic significance to Ahmici. It was a strangle-hold on the main supply route. The fighting that took place in October of 1992 was not the result of any policy of persecution by Bosnian Croats. It was a direct response to an act of aggression by the ABiH. Turning to events in Ahmici in April of 1993, as we have said throughout, the incidents in Ahmici were tragic. But the Trial Chamber's consideration needs to be who was responsible for that act, and we believe it is clear that Mr. Kordic was not the responsible person. There is no evidence that he issued any order with respect to Ahmici or otherwise undertook any act that resulted in any deaths in Ahmici. We will present limited evidence on what actually took place. We are grateful to the Prosecution, in that during their presentation of evidence, it has become clear that there was some defence that took place in Ahmici, whether it be the evidence of the increased alertedness of the troops in Ahmici on April the 15th, the evidence that's been presented as to those -- the Territorial Defence in Ahmici, and the weapons that were available to members of the Territorial Defence. But the bottom line is that Mr. Kordic was simply not responsible for anything that took place in Ahmici. There is one other village within Vitez that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Browning, according to what Mr. Sayers announced, you took the floor to speak, in the first place, about the nature of the conflict, that is, whether it was an international conflict or not. You are saying, no, it wasn't. And you said in the beginning that you were going to submit that it was not an international conflict, and you started from the idea that the criterion of the overall control, that is, the global control or what we would call global control, I understand that that is your starting point, that is, the criterion of the overall control. Could you please explain to us how you understand this overall control, since you are saying -- since you gave us only two elements, that is, that the HVO was not a puppet. That was one. Secondly, that there were no HV elements, the elements of the Croatian army, in the area and conflict that we are concerned with. These are the two things that you told us to say, that the HVO was not a puppet government, a government that was on anybody's string, that there were no HV elements there, and that, therefore, there was no -- that kind of overall control and that the nature of the conflict was not international. Is that the reasoning behind what you are saying? Because I wish to remind you that this is not quite the definition of overall control which is, at present, in the jurisprudence. The overall control is described as intervention by persons involved in a conflict at the level of the -- at the strategic level, even if the implicated army, that is, the HVO involved in an internal conflict remains the master of the tactic, even if it has a certain degree of autonomy, even if it is not only a puppet, even it is autonomous, it is, nevertheless, in the service of a strategy which was developed elsewhere. Are you going to address that point of view? Are you going to address this thesis and to respond to it? Because you are saying that there was no overall control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, the -- we believe that when the military witnesses take the stand, that it will be clear that the HVO was autonomous from the Republic of Croatia, that there was not pervasive or overall control. And as these witnesses take the stand, it will be obvious that the events that happened in Central Bosnia were not being dictated by Zagreb. That is our position, and that is what we believe the evidence will show as the testimony of the military witness takes place in this case. Let me, if I may, proceed to just briefly touch upon some of the evidence with respect to the various villages, and let me turn very quickly to the village of Divjak, which is also in the Vitez municipality. We believe there has been no evidence with regard to any sort of property damage that took place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We said that in our order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Let me proceed also to briefly touch upon Kiseljak and the events and what the evidence will show in Kiseljak. We intend to present limited evidence, either by live testimony or by transcript, with respect to Kiseljak. The bottom line with respect to Kiseljak is that Mr. Kordic had no influence in the Kiseljak area. In fact, there has been significant testimony so far about the difficulty of travelling from Busovaca to Kiseljak, and I think the testimony is very clear that that route was cut off beginning in January of 1993. We will present some testimony to reiterate that, that it was extremely difficult for anyone to travel between Busovaca and Kiseljak. As a matter of fact, the only testimony that is presented that in any way links Mr. Kordic to Kiseljak is the testimony of Witness Y, who allegedly saw Mr. Kordic for a few split seconds. That testimony, we believe, when everything is said and done and it's clear how difficult it is for someone to get from Busovaca to Kiseljak during the civil war, that testimony is simply not credible. With respect to the specific villages in Kiseljak, let me divide them very briefly into two categories, the villages along the main supply route, which would be Svinjarevo, Gomionica, Gromlijak, Bajrici, Pujuvisnica [phoen], Visnjica, and Han Ploca. Those villages were legitimate military targets, because they had strategic significance along the main supply route. The evidence that has been presented thus far makes clear that those villages were defended by ABiH, and the fact that fighting took place over a location of strategic significance simply does not rise to the level of a war crime. With respect to Rotilj, which is a village that is not precisely on the main supply route, the evidence is clear that that village was attacked by the HVO under the command of Mirko Redzo, who attacked the village because the village was being used -- houses were being used from that village to fire on HVO troops. One of the ECMM monitors, Hendrik Morsink, testified that that attack was a logical reaction and the attack on the village had clear military justifications. There has also been some indication that after the attack, Rotilj was used as a concentration camp. That myth, I think, was dispelled by the testimony of Witness AJ, who testified that there were -- although there were HVO guards at the entrance of the village, that there were no fences around it and the HVO did not even patrol within the village. His testimony, that he felt like he was kind of under house arrest, simply is not sufficient to give rise to a war crime. More importantly with respect to Rotilj, the fact that it was a village in Kiseljak, Mr. Kordic simply had -- there is no evidence, no indication that Mr. Kordic had anything -- any knowledge with respect to events in that village or that it was ever brought to his attention. I will also say the same is true with regard to Tulica, that the Prosecution contends that Tulica was attacked in June of 1993 and that eight Muslim men were executed following that attack. There is no evidence that Mr. Kordic ever knew of any crimes that occurred in Tulica, and moreover there is some question as to what was known generally within the public until the bodies were exhumed in 1998. In essence, Your Honours, we will be very brief when we present evidence on these specific villages. We will focus on the overall role of Mr. Kordic and his lack of responsibility at the highest levels of government, as well as the evidence that he was not involved in a widespread plan of persecution. Accordingly, the evidence on these specific villages, during our case in chief, will be very short and very succinct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would just like to add to what my colleague has started. My task is to very quickly delineate the events in Busovaca, starting in May 1992, and then the conflict in January of 1993, events relating to the checkpoint at Kacuni, and, in closing, several thoughts relating to the testimony of the late Midhat Haskic. This last issue is unrelated to Busovaca, but I would like to cover it in order not to get up again. As Your Honours well know, the Busovaca municipality is surrounded by the Vitez municipality on the west, Zenica on the north, and to the east Kakanj, and Kiseljak and Fojnica on the south. It is a relatively small municipality. It only covers a square area of about 149 square kilometres, and in the census of 1991, it had 18.847 population. The census figures have been presented here. I don't think that I need to belabour that point. All the events which I have touched upon earlier today, which took place in the territory of the former Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, were also reflected in the territory of Busovaca municipality. After the multi-party elections in November 1990, the three nationalist parties, the SDA, HDZ, and SDS, even before the full agreement on the cooperation was hammered out, participated in the local government. In order not to repeat what I said today, but everything that happened elsewhere, that is, all the differences which took place at the higher level were all also reflected in the political life of the Busovaca municipality. This, obviously, became exacerbated when the war broke out, because there were three military barracks of the former JNA in the territory of Busovaca. In the spring of 1992, it was clear that the war was coming and Busovaca, therefore, established a crisis staff. This was something that was provided for in the 1974 constitution. So the Busovaca municipal government formed the crisis staff, and Croats formed a very slight majority in this crisis staff. This crisis staff took the role of governing life in the Busovaca municipality, but what I want to point out is that the representatives of the Croats and Muslims in this crisis staff also made an agreement on the distribution of weapons which the former JNA held in storage in Kaonik barracks. The other two barracks are insignificant in this regard. They also divided the barracks, and the one in Kacuni went to the Muslims and the other one in Kiseljak went to -- Draga went to the Croats. Even though an agreement was reached, the Muslim side wanted to breach it, and Dzemal Merdan came, unauthorised, with some hundred people and tried to take over the control of the weapons. However, the members of the Croatian military structures prevented this, which led to the first incident which, fortunately, resulted in only two wounded. But because of this attempt at disruption, the HVO tried to establish peace and law and order, which led to the order which was Exhibit Z100 issued by the then commander of the HVO staff, Ivo Brnada, which was also signed by Mr. Kordic. He cosigned it. Following this order, on the 22nd of May, 1992, a new order was issued. This is Exhibit Z111, issued by Florijan Glavocevic and which was also cosigned by Mr. Kordic, in which an attempt is made to establish law and order and return life to normalcy. So the HVO took responsibility for the organisation of life in the territory of its own municipality. But what is important is what we have already pointed out and cross-examined the witnesses from Busovaca on, this order specifically states that the HVO is taking over the responsibility for the organisation of life until the right conditions were met when all issues would be resolved by agreement with the Muslim representatives rather than resolved by force or any other forcible means. It is our duty to prove in this case that the Muslims, as an ethnic group -- this is what was their name -- were not deprived of their rights in the Busovaca municipality in the course of 1992. For instance, even after the HVO took the control of the government in Busovaca, all Muslim employees remained in the local administrative bodies except Witness O, who stated that his job was simply phased out in the new restructuring of the organisation, and he found another job with the help of a Croat member of the HVO. During our presentation of evidence, we will show that Witness M, who here admitted that he remained an employee in the municipal government until December of 1993, even though he claimed that this was done in -- that he remained so only in a formal way, we will prove that he had equal rights, and not only did he work normally, but he was also made part of different committees that were established to handle different issues. Now, all that I have said so far has to be placed in the context of the time of the period. It was a time when the JNA and the SDS have already taken control of most of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which means that a large number of refugees flowed into the Lasva River Valley, including Busovaca municipality. On the one side, this disrupted the previous demographic structure, but what was worse was that these refugees brought with them all disillusionment, anger, and tragedy of what they had experienced from where they had come from. So all these refugees in this relatively contained area of the Lasva River Valley, and even more so in Busovaca, looked for a place to come and stay and to bring their families. At first, it created chaos, led to the commission of many criminal acts. Both the Croat and Muslim sides attempted to receive these refugees in an organised way and did so as far as they could, but the influx of the refugees was such that they were unable to control them. We will show that in one of the joint meetings in which Muslims and Croats discussed matters on an equal footing was held on 10 November 1992, and it was attended by a number of persons, some of whom have already been heard by this Trial Chamber in this case, and we will also offer testimony of others there. And just to further flesh out something that we have already addressed in the cross-examination of some witnesses, as of spring 1992 in the territory of Busovaca municipality, the HVO forces and the TO forces were operated and coexisted on an equal basis; that is, even before the armed conflict between the Croats, that is, the HVO and the TO and later ABiH, as the Court knows, the Muslims created a Presidency in Kacuni in January of 1993, and they had all other agencies such as the police, and this was testified to by both Witness A and Witness O. In our case in chief, we will show that in the area of Busovaca or throughout Herceg-Bosna, there was no organised persecution of the Muslim population. And I may just mention one detail which will show this division of territory, that this natural division, if I may call it that, of the zones of interest which was established in 1992 is still there to date, and in terms of the Busovaca municipality, this balance was at about 50/50 per cent. We will prove, further, that Mr. Kordic had no responsibility of the Busovaca municipalities. Mr. Florijan Glavocevic and Mr. Zoran Maric were in charge of the local government in Busovaca. We will also prove that Mr. Kordic had no responsibilities in the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade. It was Niko Mujezinovic and later Dusko Grubesic who were in charge of it. We will show that in the territory of Busovaca municipality, where he worked and lived, he was a member of the HDZ, and for a time he was the president of the HDZ, who was active in politics and who was fighting for one thing, which was for the rights of the Croatian people to live with other ethnic groups in that area. He was a moral authority, which he proved also through his family life. When we talk about Busovaca, my colleague Mr. Sayers also mentioned what took place in January of 1993. I will not belabour this point, but I believe that I need to refresh the memory of the testimony of Colonel Stewart, who recollected his memories of that era when he said to Enver Hadzihasanovic and Dzemal Merdan, that is, the commander of the 3rd Corps of the BiH, this time, referring to the conflict of January 1993, it was for once something that the Muslims can be blamed for. And I believe that this fact has been proven, but we will show that this conflict which was provoked by the TO and the ABiH, from that time on, the territory of Busovaca municipality was physically isolated from the Kiseljak municipality as well as Fojnica municipality. And just in brief, my colleagues have already touched upon this, but I want to just mention the first crime in middle Bosnia, the first planned crime in Dusina in which Croats were victims. However, this crime did not have an end in itself. In this conflict of January 1993, all the Croat villages which are located along the main supply route between Bilalovac and Kacuni, and I'm referring primarily to the Gusti Grab, Oseliste, Javor, Bukovci, were simply destroyed; that is, there were scores of killed Croats and many were driven out. This can be found in the milinfosum, Exhibit number 105/1. Also, we will bring a representative of the local Busovaca assembly at that time, who will testify to how his parents were killed during that conflict. Your Honours, I would like to just say a few things about the checkpoint at Kacuni. In presenting their evidence, the Prosecution did not present a single piece of evidence which would incontrovertibly link Mr. Dario Kordic to any criminal act in Busovaca. The only exception is an attempt by the Prosecutor to use an indirect way to link up our client with one of the Delija brothers in Busovaca. This was the testimony of Witness AE, who said that Mr. Dario Kordic was personally at the checkpoint in Kacuni around the 21st of January, 1993, and at that time issued a verbal threat to one of the Delija brothers, which later resulted in the death of this person in Busovaca. I do not want to analyse the statement of Witness AE, but I have to say that his testimony is completely fabricated in respect of what took place not only on the 21st of January, 1993 but also on the 24th of January, 1993, and we will prove that he did not speak truthfully on either of these two incidents. That witness, when he referred to the incident on the 21st of January, 1993, was not objective when he spoke about the direction from which the vehicle arrived and which will prove that the vehicle did not come from the direction of Kiseljak but from Busovaca, heading for Kiseljak. Secondly, that there were not three vehicles, as he claimed, but only one. And we shall also prove that in that vehicle which was stopped at the checkpoint before the road forks over to Silos, that it was the vehicle with Ignjac Kostroman, his escort Ivo Arar, and driver Miro Musa. So that was the vehicle that was intercepted and which they tried to divert in the direction of the Silo. We shall prove, through people who were there, who issued the orders to arrest Mr. Kostroman, because we shall prove that our witnesses or, rather, our people who were there heard these soldiers executing the arrest order, said explicitly they had the orders from Dzemal Merdan to arrest Mr. Kostroman. "Kica 2," [phoen] That must have been a codename. And we shall prove what we set out to prove, that Mr. Kordic was not is there on that day, and that, therefore, he simply could have nothing to do with Mirsad Delija's death. The same applies to the incident that took place at the checkpoint on the 24th of January, 1993. To cut a long story short, I shall not be quoting that witness, but I must say that he gave completely wrong information about how many vehicles there were, how many died, and so on and so forth. We shall prove that there were two vehicles rather than one on that road; secondly, that Ivica Petrovic was in the first vehicle and that he was killed, and that there were two persons in the second vehicle, which is contrary to what the Witness AE said. Also, that during the crossfire which ensued, two persons were killed rather than one, which the witness asserted. We shall also show the Court the death certificates of both of them and, thereby, we shall automatically prove that the Witness AE did not tell the truth when he said that the second survived was then escorted by Muslim forces through Busovaca, because the third one, the one who survived, survived only owing to his own ingenuity and fled not to Busovaca but to Kiseljak, that is, to the upper road. And I do not wish to tax your patience with this any longer, but this could be the end of the Busovaca part of our case, and just a couple of questions related to the testimony of witness Midhat Haskic. Your Honour admitted into evidence the statement of that witness who, unfortunately, died, and, therefore, could not be called to testify. So the Defence had to go into the facts which were pinpointed by him. I have to say that he is the only witness of some 400 witnesses who were on the Prosecutor's list of witnesses who referred to some facts which allegedly had happened in the village of Veceriska in the municipality of Vitez, notably about what happened on the 15th of April, 1993 around 2000 hours. We think that the testimony of that witness and the testimony of Witness V, who also addressed the incidents in Gornja Veceriska, at least so far in the personality of Mr. Kordic is concerned, was equally untrue, and we shall, therefore, prove that Mr. Dario Kordic was not the godfather of Ivo Miljanac's [phoen] Child, as claimed by Witness V; that Mr. Kordic never dropped by the coffee shop owned by brothers Drmic; that Mr. Kordic, likewise, never frequented that coffee shop and, therefore, could not be there on the 15th of April, 1993, in the evening of that day; and finally, that Mr. Kordic never used that military jeep in camouflage colours with an eagle painted on it that as witness Midhat Haskic claimed in his statement. Mr. Kordic -- and we shall prove that -- had nothing to do with the Gornja Veceriska village in the municipality of Vitez and what happened in April 1993 in that village. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, insofar as Stupni Do is concerned, the only evidence that connects Mr. Kordic with the events there, as you will recall, is Witness AO. We intend to introduce evidence about Witness AO, and the Court might well ask itself: Is this story to be believed? We believe the conclusions that the Court will reach will be self-evident following that evidence. In connection with Fojnica, I've already covered. Novi Travnik. We intend to introduce the testimony of two witnesses, who lived in Novi Travnik, to describe the actual situation there, and also the testimony of our military witnesses who will describe the course of the fighting there. In connection with the other particular issues, we intend to introduce evidence on the Convoy of Joy, specifically from the organisers of the Croat portion of that convoy and the organiser of the security portion of that convoy. We have other evidence relating to the Convoy of Joy as well from the military figures, specifically Major Filipovic, who was there; Brigadier Nakic, who was there; and Colonel-General Petkovic, provided he'll agree to testify. We believe the evidence on the Convoy of Joy is that there are no HVO soldiers who will establish that Mr. Kordic gave any orders or instructions relating to this convoy. He was asked to help; he did. He did his best to clean up this mess and to help the convoy pass through what was a war zone in very difficult circumstances. You've also heard much discussion from the Defence about the fact that eight small children were blown to pieces by an artillery shell on the night of June the 10th, just before the convoy was apprehended by a raging mob of civilians, and we'll show you the very gruesome videotape of that incident, unfortunately. The other items, two last items that I would care to address. Evidence was heard from an early witness, Mr. Cicak. We will give evidence regarding the lucidity of this individual. And evidence that the Court will recall -- actually, this is an appropriate subject upon which to conclude, and that is an alleged connection between a particular military unit -- you'll recall perhaps the testimony of Witness U. There's another military unit called the Scorpions, I believe, and supposedly Mr. Kordic is alleged to have a connection with this Witness U, related a conversation that he had supposedly had with a member of this unit who made some statements. We've decided to call that person to whom he spoke, and you can hear him for yourself. At the conclusion of the Defence case, Your Honour, we will submit that the Prosecution has failed to produce evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Kordic is guilty of any war crimes or serious violations of humanitarian law, and we believe that the response to the question: "Is Mr. Kordic guilty of these charges beyond a reasonable doubt," will be, "No." But also there is another question that should be asked: "Is Mr. Dario Kordic innocent?" Our respectful submission will be that he is innocent of all charges and that he should be acquitted on all counts. Thank you very much indeed for your patience, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, do I take it you've got two witnesses here, or will have for later this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We have three witnesses here, and we expect to have a fourth witness here. As I told the Court, we intend to be expeditious and move the witnesses forward, and we're going to do our best to fulfil our obligation to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you'll have to shorten the time estimate on the first one, having just looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can do that, Your Honour. We've tried -- we're working on doing the same as the Prosecution did. We've prepared extensive summaries of the evidence, and I would think that what we could do is simply present those to the Court, say that you could answer questions on a particular paragraph, have it marked as an exhibit, and just offer the witness up for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll see how we get on with that. But at some stage, we want to discuss your witness list with you, which we can do in a Status Conference, but we'll need -- at the moment, that is due to be carried out at the end of the presentation, but we will do it in such a way that we can hear as much evidence this week as possible, try and hear all your witnesses this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kovacic, tomorrow morning. How long do you anticipate you'll be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, frankly, I did prepare two versions, a short one and a longer one, and since I have the benefit, if I may say so, that the Kordic Defence has already covered all related circumstances in which all the bad things happened in Bosnia in '92 and '93, I, of course, will join them on this part of the material and could concentrate only on the part of the case which concerns only my client. I will try to extract some things this evening, but I'm quite confident that I could finish within one and a half hours maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: Half past 9.00, then, tomorrow morning.
